reason: The provided sources sufficiently support a surprising 45-second story with at least 10 claims backed by multiple sources.
story: In February 1990, the Voyager 1 spacecraft looked back toward home from over six billion kilometers away, capturing a portrait of the solar system requested by astronomer Carl Sagan. Hidden inside a ray of scattered sunlight was our entire world, appearing as a tiny, pale blue dot less than a single pixel in size. The historic photo almost never happened due to fears that pointing the cameras near the sun would destroy them, alongside years of mission resistance. Yet this single, fuzzy speck transformed our cosmic perspective forever, serving as a humbling reminder that everything we love, know, and fight over exists on a fragile mote of dust suspended in a sunbeam.
angle: Earth appears as a tiny, invisible-to-the-naked-eye speck less than a single pixel wide when photographed from over 4 billion miles away.

claims.claim: Voyager 1 took the Pale Blue Dot photograph on February 14, 1990.
The photograph was taken from a distance of over 6 billion kilometers or 4 billion miles away.
Earth appears as less than a single pixel, specifically 0.12 of a pixel.
The idea to take the picture was originally proposed by astronomer Carl Sagan in 1981.
Requests to take the photo were repeatedly rejected for years due to limited resources and the danger of pointing cameras near the Sun.
The light bands across the photograph are artifacts resulting from sunlight reflecting off parts of the camera and sunshade.
The image was part of a broader Family Portrait series consisting of 60 frames covering six or seven planets and the Sun.
After taking the images, mission managers commanded Voyager 1 to power down its cameras permanently to conserve power.
The radio signal and image data traveled at the speed of light, taking over five and a half hours to reach Earth.
NASA released a re-mastered version of the Pale Blue Dot image for its 30th anniversary in 2020.

disputed: Exact sequence of internal NASA approvals and who independently conceived the idea first alongside Sagan (such as Carolyn Porco in 1983) should be attributed to specific accounts if mentioned.
